items.body: 本誌の編集部に参加してまもないのですが、「キュレーターズノート」の原稿を読むたびに「学芸員」や「キュレーター」という職能の広さに驚かされます。例えば、ひとつの展覧会をかたちにするだけでも、膨大なインプットにはじまり、作品借用や輸送、設営をめぐる細かな調整や無数の事務作業まで、途方もない試行錯誤を経て、ようやく空間ができあがります。 今号から執筆を担当いただくアーティゾン美術館の内海潤也さんは、東京都写真美術館でのインターン時代、展覧会の「物理的条件に立脚しつつ、考えを展開しなくてはいけないのだと痛感」したと振り返ります。そして「思想や理論も、空間、予算、時間、安全性、輸送、保全、そして多くの人の労働を通って、初めて展覧会のかたち」になる、と言います。 つまりキュレーターの仕事は、空間に作品を立ち上げる物理的な仕事であり、非常に身体的な側面があるのです。同じく「キュレーターズノート」の著者である、福岡市美術館の忠あゆみさんもまた、自身の3歳の子どもが、展示された絵を「しかくい『え』はきらい」と話したことに端を発して、展覧会と身体について思いを巡らせました。 忠さんは最後に「子どもが『きらい』と言っていたのは、絵画ではなく自分の身体が入り込めない鑑賞の形式だった」と結んでいます。鑑賞するときに、そこに直接的な身体の接触はありません。しかし、誰かがつくった作品を、見知らぬ誰かに届ける仕事の根底には、そこにない「誰かの身体」を想像しながら空間を編む技術があるのだと、両氏の言葉から受け取りました。（s）

items.excerpt: 東京と京都にて、SDレビュー2026「第44回 建築・環境・インテリアのドローイングと模型の入選展」が開催されます。 SDレビューは、実際に「建てる」という厳しい現実のなかで、設計者がひとつの明確なコンセプトを導き出す思考の過程を、ドローイングと模型によって示そうというものです。1982年に建築家・槇文彦氏の発案のもとに第1回目が開催され、以降毎年「建築・環境・インテリアのドローイングと模型」の展覧会とその誌上発表が行なわれています。 第44回となる今回は、入選作品（計12作品）が公開され、10月には京都にて公開プレゼンテーションも開催予定です。 詳細は、下記および公式サイトをご覧ください。 ＜アドバイザー＞ 隈研吾 ＜審査員＞ 山梨知彦、冨永祥子、満田衛資、増田信吾 ＜入選作品＞ ・「死なない建築、ずっと建てられている建築を目指して」イ・ヘドゥン＋チェ・ジェピル ・「都市に触れる」太田雄太郎 ・「崖にひそむ幽かな住まい」小林玲子＋今和泉 拓＋杵家里紗子＋遠山大輝 ・「大径木の子ども食堂」佐々木勝敏＋藤野なみか ・「ORGAN」鈴木岳彦 ・「Iプロジェクト」寺本健一＋光本直人＋濱名直子

items.body: “Singing my songs I hold dear; from my virtual world to yours” – Isekaijoucho Hello there! And welcome to the J-Music Exchange/Rate! If you know exactly what that means and what we’re all about here, you should also be well aware what to do from here on out, so off you go! However, if this is actually your first time here and you’re not entirely sure what you just walked into, please give the following primer a quick read: The Exchange/Rate is a tandem album review series conducted every month by yours truly alongside my good friend and fellow Japanese music fan Al (from Omunibasu). Each month we decide on a specific theme with which our reviews would revolve around. We then pick out albums from our respective libraries which we think best coincides with that theme. We will then give the album we chose to the other person and vice versa (exchange), after which we then listen to and subsequently review the album we were given (rate). This project has not only allowed us to explore music beyond our libraries, but it provides an opportunity for us to see our favorite albums from a different point of view. It is our hope that this series is able to do the same for you and that you either find a new artist to try out and/or we offer you a fresh take on one of *your* favorite albums This month it was my turn again to dish out a theme. I think I came up with a pretty interesting one specifically within the context of the Exchange/Rate. and that is bands/artists we started listening to thanks to the Exchange/Rate! I think when Al and I first started doing this series, the most obvious way of looking at the “exchange” part of the Exchange/Rate was simply through the albums we gave each other. I send him something I think he’d find interesting, he does the same for me, and every month we both hopefully walk away having listened to something we otherwise might not have checked out on our own. But after years of doing this, I think it’s fair to say that the exchange goes quite a bit further than that. We’ve talked about a plethora of artists between the two of us at this point, whether through the albums we’ve directly exchanged, comparisons made during reviews, conversations outside of the series, or simply repeatedly exposing each other to certain names until eventually curiosity gets the better of us. Naturally, some of those artists have stuck around long after their respective Exchange/Rate appearances, becoming part of our regular listening habits in the process. So this month, we thought it’d be fun to look at a couple of those artists and see where that influence has taken us. On my end I went ahead and handed Al Soul/R&B artist MALIYA’s album pluto for him to go over with you guys at the Omunibasu Substack (check it out here!). Al in turn had me revisit the one and only Isekaihoucho’s Shikisai for me to talk about and review. So, without further ado, let us enter Isekaijoucho’s world! ーー Isekaijoucho (ヰ世界情緒) is a Japanese virtual singer affiliated with the artist collective KAMITSUBAKI STUDIO, as well as a member of the virtual singer group Virtual Witch Phenomenon, better known as V.W.P. Described as a “virtual dark singer,” Isekaijoucho aims to express the world through her songs and creative works, often weaving themes of darkness and light together through her distinctively powerful yet ethereal singing voice. Beyond music, she’s also a multifaceted creator who expresses herself through a number of different mediums, including illustration, narration, and voice acting. ＜Ｓｈｉｋｉｓａｉ (色彩)＞(＊Spotify link to the full album) CDJapan Affiliate Link(s):N/A ＜T ｒａｃｋｌｉｓｔ＞ ０１・息吹/ibuki -instrumental-０２・そして白に還る/soshite shiro ni kaeru０３・ラピスのお人形/lapis no oningyou０４・パンドラコール/pandora call０５・ディメンション/dimension０６・キミ消失セカイ/kimi shoushitsu sekai０７・グレイスケイル/grayscale０８・此処に棘と死を/koko ni toge to shi o０９・ネリネの内緒事/nerine no naishogoto１０・暮れなずむ約束/kurenazumu yakusoku１１・ヴァーミリオン/vermillion１２・描き続けた君へ/kaki wo tsudxuketa kimi e１３・かたちなきもの/katachinakimono１４・ANGELIC１５・色彩-instrumental- Ａｌ：I first knew about Isekaijoucho through Leap’s various recommendations, but most prevalently within the Exchange/Rate segment, when I reviewed V.W.P’s first full-length album. And similar to being introduced to a brand new idol group, it was neat to learn about all these different personalities and think about how much KAMITSUBAKI struck digital gold when assembling this vocal superteam. And while I’ve come to really appreciate all of them and what they bring to the unit, Isekaijoucho was the one member that caught my eye the most. Given that visuals are important in the world of virtual talents, I’d imagine that a lot of people, myself included, gravitated towards the cute appeal of her design. But looks can be (somewhat) deceiving, as I quickly realized just how much of a fantastic and nuanced singer she really is. As many have pointed out, Joucho has excelled at performing more operatic songs, adding to the dramatic theatrics through her eeriely calm demeanor and ability to sing to the high heavens when needed. And I do think that her most recent full-length album, Colors, exemplifies that visual/auditory contrast of hers and much more. Songs like “Lapis no Ohitogata” and “Pandora Call” have always stood out to me for its mysterious attractiveness and how it fits Joucho’s personality pretty nicely. But what I found most interesting about this record is her apparent desire to expand her range, as we later hear Joucho perform on tracks that stray a bit farther from her usual stuff. Obviously, you can tell that she holds her own on those heavier rock tracks; but listening to her take on various styles like a jazzy musical number, a touching piano ballad, or even something you’d normally hear Harusaruhi rap on… it’s all an impressive display of who Joucho is as an evolving singer and the heights that she’s very well capable of reaching. I have always had a lot of admiration for faceless talents, as they’ve proven that revealing your real identity is not always a necessity in the world of public/online entertainment. And while I never was really caught up in the massive ‘virtual talent’ wave we’ve been seeing over the years, no doubt has it given people endless ways to express themselves through their pursuits of content creation, gaming, art, and especially music. And with how Joucho has presented herself in this album, it’s hard not to see her as a prime example of that type of creative talent. ＜Ｓｏｎｇｓ ｏｆ Ｉｎｔｅｒｅｓｔ＞ ０１・息吹/Ibuki -instrumental-、０２・そして白に還る/soshite shiro ni kaeruI do find it a little funny that this is now the second album in a row we’ve reviewed here on the Exchange/Rate that begins with a dedicated instrumental opener (lol). For what it’s worth though, and as I mentioned last month, I actually enjoy these quite a bit when they’re used to lead directly into the first proper song on an album, which is once again the case here with Ibuki and Soshite Shiro ni Kaeru. Ibuki opens with this grand choir hymn that immediately gives the album an almost mystical, high-fantasy feel. That imagery only becomes stronger as the orchestral accompaniment gradually comes into view, complete with sweeping strings and blaring horns that make it feel as though we’re standing at the beginning of some grand hero’s adventure. It’s brief, but it does exactly what I would want an opening instrumental like this to do; set the scene before seamlessly handing things off to what comes next. Fittingly enough, the choir then gives way to Isekaijoucho’s own beautiful hymn at the beginning of Soshite Shiro ni Kaeru. And I think it’s at around this point that anyone who isn’t terribly familiar with Joucho, or perhaps only knows her through some of the covers she’s done over the years, might start to realize that she’s actually a bit of a singing virtuoso. I don’t just mean that in the sense that she has a good voice either. I personally think she does, of course, though I can also understand her particular tonality perhaps being an acquired taste for some. What impresses me more is the sheer amount of control she has over it. There’s an almost uncanny precision to the way she moves between notes, adjusts the weight behind her voice, and knows exactly how much of it to use at any given moment. I honestly wouldn’t be surprised to learn that she’s had some form of classical training in the past, though I’d probably be even more impressed if she hasn’t. There’s just this innate sense of grandeur to the way she sings that makes performances like this feel remarkably natural for her. You get a pretty good sense of all of that listening to Soshite Shiro ni Kaeru, which, in my opinion, is Isekaijoucho very much in her element. Give Joucho a huge instrumental arrangement and enough room to make use of the technical range at her disposal, and she has an incredible ability to rise right alongside it rather than getting swallowed up by everything happening around her; a dynamic that I’ve always found particularly fascinating about her music. ０７・グレイスケイル/grayscaleWhich is kinda funny when you then arrive at Grayscale around the midway point of the album, as it sounds almost nothing like Soshite Shiro ni Kaeru. This is, of course, very much by design, as I’m sure a lot of you have probably clued in on as well. I’ll talk a little more later about what I think Grayscale represents within the broader context of Shikisai, but to give you guys a bit of a hint, it does dovetail into both the visual and auditory narrative that the album appears to be building. At the very least, I don’t think its placement here is simply for the sake of giving listeners a breather before heading into the album’s latter half. Going back to the song itself though, if I’m being completely honest, I didn’t really know what to make of it during my first couple of spins through the album. Initially, I mostly chalked it up to some of KAMITSUBAKI’s broader musical tendencies bleeding into Isekaijoucho’s own work, given the group’s penchant for electronic music and rap, both of which I’m also a fan of. After a while though, Grayscale started tickling a part of my brain that I haven’t really ventured into for the longest time. The more I listened to it, the more it began reminding me of an artist I listened to a ton when I was first getting into Japanese music; specifically, old-school DAOKO from her indie days under LOW HIGH WHO? There’s something about the quick, almost spoken-word style of rap that Joucho employs here that takes me back to that period of DAOKO’s music, where her delivery would almost casually tumble across the beat rather than approaching it like a more conventional rap performance. And I think that’s what ultimately got me to appreciate Grayscale quite a bit more than I initially did. Her youthful voice and demeanor aside, Isekaijoucho has always struck me as a consummate professional through and through. A track like this takes her considerably further away from the grand, technically demanding vocal performances that I personally associate with her, yet she never comes across as uncomfortable doing it. If anything, I thought she acquitted herself remarkably well, adapting her delivery to what the song asks of her without making it feel like she’s merely trying on a style for novelty’s sake. It’s certainly not the version of Isekaijoucho I expected to hear after the way Shikisai begins, but given what the album is seemingly trying to accomplish, I have a feeling that’s precisely the point. ０８・此処に棘と死を/koko ni toge to shi woThis middle portion of Shikisai is actually my favorite stretch of the album to go through. Not only does it provide a nice stylistic shakeup around the halfway point, but I also think it makes for just about the best demonstration of Isekaijoucho’s versatility as a singer. You really only have to look at the jump from Grayscale to Koko ni Toge to Shi wo to see what I mean. Circling back to something I mentioned at the very beginning, Joucho, in my opinion, is truly right at home performing against these big, theatrical orchestral arrangements. There’s almost a Broadway-esque quality to her delivery here, particularly in the way she’s able to rise to meet the scale and drama of the instrumentation around her. And again, I think part of why this works so well comes from the contrast inherent to Isekaijoucho herself. If you were to hear her speaking voice or even just look at her character design, you probably wouldn’t immediately expect this kind of performance from her. Her voice naturally comes across as incredibly dainty and fragile, and I’ll even concede that there are singers out there with stronger natural vocal qualities than her. But that’s where I think the distinction between having a great voice and being a great singer becomes incredibly important. Because whatever Joucho might lack in natural vocal power, she more than makes up for through sheer technique. That’s perhaps my favorite thing about her as a performer. As delicate as she might look and sound, at no point does Isekaijoucho ever truly feel outsized by the music around her. You can put these massive strings, pounding percussion, and all sorts of theatrical flourishes behind her, and somehow she always finds a way to make herself feel every bit as important to the arrangement. Of course, credit for that doesn’t belong solely to Joucho. Vocaloid producer SLAVE.V-V-R, making their sole contribution to Shikisai here, gives her one hell of a composition to work with. More broadly though, I also have to give KAMITSUBAKI STUDIO a lot of credit for seemingly understanding exactly what makes Isekaijoucho such an interesting vocalist and continually putting her in musical situations where those qualities can shine. １２・描き続けた君へ/kaki tsudzuketa kimi eIn my initial draft for this review, I thought I was gonna have a hard time deciding on one final song to feature before giving my overall impressions on the album. But after giving Shikisai a fair number of spins, I eventually realized that I couldn’t bring myself not to cap everything off with Kaki Tsudzuketa Kimi e. For one, in as much as I really enjoy the theatrical presentation of something like Koko ni Toge to Shi wo, part of me believes that this kind of electro chamber pop arrangement is where Isekaijoucho could ultimately find a lot of mainstream success. There’s this grand, almost epic quality to the song that I could very easily imagine translating to a big game or anime tie-up, while still retaining enough of the characteristics that make Joucho’s music feel distinctly her own. More importantly for this review though, I also think Kaki Tsudzuketa Kimi e serves as a perfectly positioned capstone performance for just about everything we’ve talked about thus far regarding Joucho’s prowess as a singer. While I’d probably still say Koko ni Toge to Shi wo is my favorite song off Shikisai as a whole, the stretch from around 3:23 through the end of Kaki Tsudzuketa Kimi e might just be my favorite sequence on the entire album. Everything about it is just gorgeous. I love how quickly the melody moves and evolves over such a short span of time, constantly giving Joucho something new to respond to as the arrangement builds toward its conclusion. And respond she does, because she absolutely steals the show here. After an entire album spent demonstrating just how much control she has over her voice, Joucho finally gets this extended vocal run where it feels like she’s letting everything loose at once. It’s become one of those moments that I actively look forward to whenever I put the song on. ＜Ｗｈａｔ Ｉ ｔｈｉｎｋ ｏｆ Ｓｈｉｋｉｓａｉ ＞ If you’re a longtime reader of the blog and follower of the Exchange/Rate series, then you should already be well familiar with the term “grab bag”. As a quick refresher, a “grab bag” is what Al and I have taken to calling albums that showcase a number of different musical styles, as opposed to something more uniform that’s built predominantly around a singular style or sound signature. Over the years since we first started using the term, we’ve revisited the concept across a number of different reviews, attempting to further define not only what makes an album a grab bag, but also why an artist might choose to make one and, perhaps more importantly, who exactly they’re meant for. It’s quite honestly become one of my favorite recurring concepts to revisit as part of the Exchange/Rate. Mostly because, as much as Al and I have talked about grab bags over the years, our understanding of them continues to evolve as we encounter albums that approach the idea in different ways. And wouldn’t you know it, we’re gonna be doing that again here with Isekaijoucho’s Shikisai. Shikisai translates rather simply to “colors,” specifically referring to color as we perceive it through light and its different wavelengths. With that in mind, something I find immediately interesting about the album, and something you’ve probably already noticed just by looking at its artwork, is that despite what a title like Shikisai might lead you to expect, the album itself isn’t something I would necessarily describe as colorful. If anything, it’s overwhelmingly white. But that’s also where I think the conceptual brilliance of Shikisai starts to reveal itself, because white isn’t actually the absence of color. Rather, when we’re talking about light, white is what we perceive when all of its different colors come together. And suddenly, the way Shikisai sounds begins to make a whole lot more sense. Because make no mistake, Shikisai is absolutely a grab bag. Across the album, you can hear Isekaijoucho moving between grand orchestral compositions, electronic music, rap, chamber pop, and plenty of other ideas in between. On the surface, these can seem like wildly different directions for the same album to take. Like, we only have to look back at Grayscale immediately followed by Koko ni Toge to Shi wo to see just how dramatic those differences can become. But I don’t think those differences are incidental. I think they’re the entire point. Each style effectively becomes another color for Isekaijoucho to inhabit. Taken individually, they’re all distinct from one another, sometimes drastically so. Bring all of them together, however, and they begin to form the white that defines Shikisai visually. The one constant holding all of those colors together, of course, is Joucho herself, who is appropriately clad in white. ＜Ｍｙ Ｒａｔｉｎｇ＞４.５ ｏｕｔ ｏｆ ５ ＆ ９ ｏｕｔ ｏｆ １０ Which brings me back to why I’ve spent so much of this review talking about her ability as a singer. Whether you give her something theatrical and orchestral like Soshite Shiro ni Kaeru or Koko ni Toge to Shi wo, ask her to rap on something as comparatively unconventional as Grayscale, or give her the soaring electro chamber pop of Kaki Tsudzuketa Kimi e, Isekaijoucho continually finds a way to adapt herself to whatever the composition asks of her. And I think that’s ultimately the biggest takeaway we’re meant to have from Shikisai. Not necessarily that Isekaijoucho has the greatest voice you’ll ever hear, because as I’ve mentioned throughout this review, that’s not really the argument I’m trying to make. Rather, what makes Joucho such an exceptional vocalist is what she’s capable of doing with that voice. Technique, control, adaptability, and an almost uncanny ability to understand what a song needs from her; throw just about any color at Isekaijoucho and she’ll find some way to make it hers. ーー What are your guys’ thoughts on Isekaijoucho’s Shikisai? Let us know in the comments! Likewise, if there are any bands or artists you started listening to thanks to the Exchange/Rate over the years, please share those with us too! We’d love to know! Lastly, before I let you guys go, don’t forget to check out Al’s review of pluto by MALIYA over at the Omunibasu Substack if you haven’t yet! Happy Listening!

items.body: Dana Vynnytska ordered an Indian harmonium, a keyboard worked by a hand-pumped bellows, at a point when she’d just started to see light again after a hard stretch, and sat with the instrument alone until melodies began to surface. What came out of those sessions became “Będę Szczęśliwa” (“I Will Be Happy”), the first single from DAGADANA‘s sixth studio album, Lumen. DAGADANA is built around Vynnytska and Daga Gregorowicz, a Polish and Ukrainian duo who write and sing in both languages, once Bartosz Nazaruk wrapped an afro-funk-inspired beat around Vynnytska’s chords and Mikołaj Pospieszalski slid a bass line underneath. Polish and Ukrainian verses trade off across “Będę Szczęśliwa,” each one answering the other, both circling back to the same picture of a river, all bends and sudden current, and a woman learning to swim with it instead of fighting it. “Gdy odpuszczam jestem kołem. Uratuję nas oboje,” Vynnytska sings at the turn of the song, “When I let go, I become the wheel. I’ll save us both,” a line she wrote out of her own experience of forgiving, herself first, then somebody else, to find her way back to that light. Gregorowicz puts it even simpler: happiness starts the moment you drop a grudge instead of carrying it around. That’s a long way from where DAGADANA started, back in 2006, when Gregorowicz and Vynnytska met at a jazz workshop in Kraków and began singing together before either of them had a band name for it. Pospieszalski and Nazaruk joined not long after, and the four of them have spent eighteen years since turning that meeting into a Fryderyk, Poland’s top music industry award, festival stages from Glastonbury to Oslo World, tours through 34 countries that took them from the Moroccan desert to Beijing’s Forbidden City, and “Jesień, Tańcuj,” the song they co-wrote for the Oscar-nominated film Chłopi. “Będę Szczęśliwa” is pulled from Lumen, Latin for light, their sixth studio album, still without a confirmed release date. The band has said it’s a step away from the folk sound that built their name. Pospieszalski produced the single himself; Mateusz Hulbój mixed it and Rafał Smoleń mastered it. Sandra Matyszewska shot and directed the video alongside Gregorowicz and Vynnytska, at Folwark Konny Hermanów, a horse farm on the Warta River in western Poland. Stream “Będę szczęśliwa” HERE and follow DAGADANA on their official website for updates on Lumen. The post Daily Discovery: DAGADANA – Będę Szczęśliwa appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.album: Trancemaster 1992-1999
items.body:
It's been four years since the last Portals feature (what kind of Portal is that?!). As a quick reminder, this series serves as my way to highlight a specific concept or deep dive into an aspect of music I enjoy, no matter the style. We've had Power Ambient, New New Age, Music For Sleeping, a reinterpretation of the KLF's Chill Out, and Classic Trance Loops amongst others. 

 For this next episode, we're going back into the world of Trance music again. Maybe our latest Trance-infused release with Mikkel Rev was the inspiration to get another Portals going after that 4-year absence... 

 Throughout the 1990s, the Trancemaster compilation series documented that evolution of the genre in real time. Across sprawling multi-disc releases, it brought together records from the emerging edges of trance, techno and progressive music (even some random nu-wave track I found), tracks that were often difficult to find outside specialist record shops and European clubs at the time, placing them into a shared world. 

 Before trance became a global industry, it was a sound still figuring out what it wanted to be. For many listeners, Trancemaster was a map of an evolving landscape that despite being called Trance, still shifted through variations of ambient, chill downtempo and techno, through its early themed compilations such as 'The Goa Gap, 'Tribal Chill Out' and 'Aural Brainfood' to name just a few. which soon dissolved into general Trancemaster compilations as the genre continued to find its sound. 

 Follow the names buried in these compilations and you could disappear into entire labels, scenes, cities and new strains of electronic music. Across the decades, the series captured Trance as it moved from something darker, stranger and more experimental into the soaring melodies and enormous emotional architecture that would eventually fill clubs around the world in the early 00's, with the label behind the compilation "Vision Soundcarriers" eventually calling it a day on the series in 2012 (citing piracy no less). 

 The result of this series is a catalog of hundreds of tracks, that became a definitive blueprint of the genre. Unknown gems and deep digs feature alongside many of the biggest classic hits you can think of (BBE, Three Drives, Lustral, Gouryella , Tiesto, etc all sit alongside the many unknowns). 

 For this edition of Portals, I've dug through the entire Trancemaster compilations through the early years of 1992–1999 (numbers 01 to 23 to be exact - the best years, dare I say?). Seven years of records that helped define a genre, and a reminder of just how wide, weird, and beautiful Trance once was. This true excavation led me into many different places, and it was interesting to see how the sound evolved over the years (especially when compared to the compilations post year 2000). 

 The Chill Out Room vibe was still apparent, and tracks were being spun by José Padilla (I remember the Max 404 track appearing after an ad break in José’s 1993 Essential Mix). Acid house was still a massive influence, with Choice, Josh Wink and many more creating head-buzzing anthems of the time. And the Goa Trance sound was still gloriously shifting BPMs to keep everyone guessing as to what went down in those far-away hedonistic times. 

 Dolphins, didgeridoos, that distinct bird sound from FSOL (!), chanted mantras and German spoken-word — Trancemaster has all the wonderful excess of a scene discovering just how far it could go, with little sense of the impact it would have. Beneath those unmistakable fingerprints of the era lies an extraordinary run of music: strange, euphoric, hypnotic and, at its best, remarkably timeless. Here are a few gems and personal favorites that capture just how broad Trance could be at the time, from ambient and downtempo, to techno, acid, progressive and the more euphoric sound that would eventually come to define it.

items.body: Of course, this trio is a supergroup, like so many of pianist Vijay Iyer’s latest ensembles. Percussionist Dafnis Prieto may be less well-known, but the now 82-year-old saxophonist and flutist Henry Threadgill is all the more so. Despite his age, he has been more productive and acclaimed than ever. He won the Pulitzer Prize for his most important work of the past 15 years, In for a Penny, In for a Pound (Zooid; 2015). It’s possibly the most consistent realization of Threadgill’s compositional system, in which he works with predetermined interval sequences that provide the musicians with a harmonic and melodic framework within which they are also expected to improvise - that is, improvisation itself becomes part of a highly complex composition. What’s fascinating about this is that the music initially seems almost chaotic, but is in fact organized with extraordinary precision. As intellectually fascinating as this music is on the one hand, it has also faced criticism on the other hand, that the whole thing is too contrived and too lifeless, too close to new classical avant-garde music. That kind of criticism can certainly not applied to “Fifteen”. The album title refers to the number of years that have passed since this trio first came together at a benefit event for the New York Jazz Gallery. Here, all three compose and improvise; recurring melodic patterns are readily - even eagerly - embraced, bringing the music closer to mainstream jazz than to free jazz. This is primarily due to Dafnis Prieto’s Cuban influences and his light, elastic groove, which remains free and almost impossible to count. This is perhaps most clearly evident in “I Want a Map”, which comes across more like a rock song, with Threadgill’s saxophone initially taking up the melody, which is developed by the piano and built up relatively straightforwardly by the drums to a crescendo. Rarely has Threadgill sounded so accessible; he uses a fair amount of growl, and his clear sound from the Air years is barely recognizable. But he wouldn’t be Henry Threadgill if he didn’t gradually incorporate small atonal elements and offbeat shifts that disrupt the piece’s static structure. Things get significantly wilder on “Fire City“, then. Prieto plays less to the beat. Here, he actually acts more like a free jazz drummer. Iyer, too, plays fewer tonal harmonies, and Threadgill’s sound is indeed clearer and more abstract on this track. The piece is denser, less airy than others on the album, but perhaps that’s precisely what makes it the most exciting, as it gallops off in different directions several times without ever losing its way. The most unusual track is the album’s finale, “On the Way”. Here, the different compositional and improvisational logics stand in direct contrast to one another: Henry Threadgill’s carefully balanced vocabulary meets the rhythmic power and temporal sophistication of Iyer and Prieto, opening up spaces for dense ensemble polyrhythms and incisive solo passages. At times, you can literally tap your foot along - you almost feel like dancing. Who would ever have expected that from an album featuring Henry Threadgill? This is definitely one of the albums that will appear on many year-end charts. Fifteen is available on vinyl, as a CD and as a download. You can listen to it and buy it on Vijay Iyer’s bandcamp site: Fifteen by Henry Threadgill, Vijay Iyer, Dafnis Prieto Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: Label: April Records, 2026 Personnel - Emil De Waal: drums, percussion; Henriette Groth: clarinet; Gustaf Ljunggren: contra alto clarinet, viola, arco contra bass, guitars; Jacob Anderskov: piano, spinet; Randi Laubek: vocals (#3,7). Danish drummer and composer Emil De Waal releases the fourth album with his brainchild group Old News. Formed in 2013, the band reunites for a new chapter that serves as a tribute to one of its former members, clarinetist and actor Elith “Nulle” Nykjær, who passed away in 2023. Novelties is informed by traditional elements, a strong sense of collective unity, and unrestrained improvisation. “ Hellen ” opens the album with a conspicuous classical influence, waltzing gently in a mid-slow tempo. Gustaf Ljunggren contributes focused bass lines on contra-alto clarinet, while Jacob Anderskov caresses the piano with smooth, delicate gestures. De Waal’s understated brushwork provides gentle, flowing propulsion, and guest clarinetist Henriette Groth emerges with a velvety tone that perfectly complements the atmosphere. The band is equally adept at navigating shifts when traditional American sounds come into play on “ Scrap Rag ” and “ Last Millennium When We Were Young ”. The former, countrified by Ljunggren’s guitar, develops an appealing Americana feel, while the latter is an elated tune steeped in positive nostalgia, where the tonal contrast between contra-alto clarinet and piano makes the entire piece glow. Both “ I Am Nobody ” and “ Forgotten Anne ” feature Danish singer-songwriter Randi Laubek, whose luminous guitar chords blend beautifully with Groth’s clarinet on the former, a gentle folk ballad that gradually reaches an atmospheric emotional apex. She wrote the latter track for the cinematic adventure-platform game of the same name. De Waal’s control of the toms is on full display on “ Flod ”, which feels ethereal on the surface yet remains firmly grounded at its core. “ Lim ”, surrounded by a bright aura in 3/4, evokes John Surman’s weightless voyages propelled by colorful brushed drumming, while “ Tightrope ” brings the immensity of Nordic soundscapes to the fore, featuring beautiful, erudite interplay between the clarinet players and a piano motif that, running diligently beneath them, defines the harmonic path. This piece is followed by “ Forgotten, Not Forgiven” , which follows the same principle while intensifying the modal atmosphere through clever tonal shifts. De Waal’s focused, well-delineated storytelling flourishes through sounds and textures that steadily draw us in. A signature stylist, he effortlessly creates an organic weave by retaining the most compelling elements of the past while giving them a fresh, atmospheric spin, allowing these compositions to unfold with a natural harmonic breath. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Hellen ► 03 - I Am Nobody ► 08 - Tightrope ► 09 - Forgotten, Not Forgiven

items.body:
JENNIE is taking her relationship with adidas to the next level.

After years of fronting campaigns and representing the brand as an ambassador, the global artist has stepped into the role of co-designer for her first collaborative collection with adidas Originals. adidas Originals by JENNIE launches globally on 1 September.

Built around the concept of "Functional Grace", the collection brings together the softness and precision of ballet with adidas' performance-inspired design language. JENNIE's take adds a futuristic edge, balancing graceful silhouettes with pieces designed for everyday wear.

“With this collaboration, I wanted to reinterpret the classic identity of adidas Originals through my own perspective and energy,” JENNIE shared. “My goal was to bring together the softness and restraint found in ballet, as well as the strength behind it, with the feeling of an endless and unknown space.”

That idea extends to the collection's Cosmic Ballerina: Kinematics campaign, which places ballet-inspired movement in a dreamlike environment influenced by the cosmos. The concept transforms ballet from a visual reference into an expression of strength, freedom, and possibility.

At the centre of the collection is the SUPERSTAR SQ BALLET, JENNIE's reinterpretation of the adidas Superstar. Inspired by the shape of a ballet pointe shoe, the footwear features a squared toe, premium leather upper, lambskin lining, ribbon detailing, and removable laces for different styling options.

The collection also features reworked track tops and pants, layering T-shirts, wrap skirts, knit wrap cardigans, sheer sleeveless bodysuits and leggings, as well as polar fleece half-zip hoodies. High-knit leg warmers and cut-out socks round out the ballet-informed wardrobe.

The adidas Originals by JENNIE FW26 collection will be available from 1 September via the adidas CONFIRMED app, select retailers, and the following adidas stores in Singapore:

adidas Brand Centre Orchard

adidas Suntec City

adidas VivoCity Performance (L1)

adidas Originals VivoCity (B1)

adidas Marina Bay Sands

adidas Jewel

adidas Bugis+

adidas Changi T1

adidas Changi T2

The collection will also be available online via adidas' dedicated JENNIE page.

items.body:
The Pokémon World Championships will make its Singapore debut from 13 to 15 August, bringing some of the world's top competitive Pokémon players together for three days of battles.

The annual tournament will take place at Singapore EXPO, before culminating in Championship Sunday at the Singapore Indoor Stadium.

The news was revealed during the closing ceremony of the 2026 Pokémon World Championships in San Francisco on 30 August. The upcoming edition will mark the first time Singapore hosts the global competition.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Pokémon (@pokemon)

Considered the pinnacle of competitive Pokémon play, the Pokémon World Championships sees players from around the world compete for World Champion titles, prizes, and other rewards across games including the Pokémon Trading Card Game, Pokémon Video Game Championships, and Pokémon GO.

This year's Pokémon World Championships also came with a musical surprise courtesy of Ed Sheeran.

The British singer-songwriter made a surprise appearance during the tournament's finale, performing one of his own songs before treating fans to the theme song from the original Pokémon anime.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by CNET (@cnet)

Sheeran is no stranger to the world of Pokémon. A longtime fan of the franchise, the singer has collaborated with Pokémon over the years through commercials, music videos, and games.

His latest appearance added a fitting musical moment to the festivities as the Pokémon World Championships prepares to head to Singapore for its next edition.

The Singapore reveal was one of several announcements made during the championships.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Play! Pokémon (@playpokemon)

An animated feature-length movie, Pokémon: Wild Card, is slated for release in early 2027, while Z Mega Evolutions — special powered-up upgrades for battles — will arrive in Pokémon Champions from 9 September.

Further details surrounding the Singapore edition of the Pokémon World Championships are expected to be announced at a later date.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by The Kallang (@thekallang.sg)

items.body:
Singapore’s live music landscape is getting a new addition.

Live Nation Singapore has announced Grange House, a new purpose-built live entertainment venue located in the heart of Orchard Road. The 3,000-capacity space is set to open by mid-2027, filling the space between Singapore’s smaller live venues and its large-scale arenas and stadiums.

Developed with support from the Singapore Tourism Board, Grange House will be open to all promoters and event organisers, creating more opportunities for artists, tours, and cultural experiences to take place in Singapore.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Grange House (@grangehousesg)

The venue was designed by Blueprint Studio, Live Nation’s in-house design and development team, with a focus on acoustics and sightlines alongside hospitality, food and drink options, and artist facilities built to international touring standards.

Beyond concerts, Grange House is also envisioned as an everyday community space. Plans include a landscaped terrace, an all-day café and restaurant, and spaces for talks, podcasts, and public events. A walkway connecting 313@Somerset to the venue will also host rotating art, exhibitions, and pop-ups.

“Singapore has been an important market for Live Nation since launching in 2006,” shared Edward Liu, Managing Director of Live Nation Singapore. “We continue to see enormous potential for live entertainment in Singapore, and Grange House is the next step in that journey.”

The new venue will form part of the continued rejuvenation of Orchard Road in collaboration with Lendlease Global Commercial REIT. According to Live Nation, its year-round live entertainment, cultural experiences, and community programming are intended to give both locals and visitors more reasons to spend time in the precinct.

Stephanie Bax, President, Venue Development for Live Nation Asia, added that Grange House was designed around “an exceptional experience for artists and fans” while maintaining a strong connection with the surrounding community.

With room for 3,000 fans and a location right in Singapore’s central shopping belt, Grange House is set to add another option to the city’s live entertainment circuit when it opens in mid-2027.

items.body:
KATSEYE's Sophia Laforteza will sit out the European and UK leg of THE WILDWORLD TOUR as she continues to focus on her health and well-being.

In an update shared on 30 August, HYBE x Geffen Records confirmed that the Filipina singer will not participate in the group's upcoming shows from 1 to 17 September.

"Sophia is focusing on her well-being, and the company remains fully committed to providing her with all the support and resources needed," the label shared.

"We sincerely ask for EYEKONS' warm understanding, as our highest priority will always be the health and long-term well-being of our artists," the statement continued. "We will share further updates as they become available. Please continue to send your love, warmth, and support to Sophia and KATSEYE."

Sophia later addressed EYEKONS herself via Instagram Stories, sharing that while she wanted to join her bandmates on tour, she needed to put her health first.

"I can't express enough how much i want to participate in this tour and perform for you all," she wrote, before adding that she has to remind herself that her health and mental well-being should come first.

The 23-year-old also shared that she has been undergoing "ongoing treatment" and doing what she can to remain healthy, occupied, and happy during her break.

"You can't pour from an empty cup," Sophia wrote.

She went on to express her gratitude to EYEKONS for their support and asked fans to continue supporting the rest of KATSEYE while she recovers.

Sophia's absence from the European and UK shows follows the announcement of her temporary hiatus earlier in August. At the time, HYBE x Geffen Records said she would step back from promotional activities to focus on her physical and mental health.

According to the label, medical professionals advised Sophia to take "dedicated time for extended rest and ongoing care to ensure a full recovery," with her health set to be reassessed in September.

Her fellow KATSEYE members have also publicly expressed their support for Sophia, as well as Manon Bannerman, who has been on hiatus since February.

"As KATSEYE, it's so important to us to always prioritize our well-being," Lara Raj told reporters following the group's performance on 14 August. "We stand by Sophia and Manon through and through. We ride for them."

"We love you guys so much, always," she added.

Further updates on Sophia's activities are expected as her recovery continues.

items.body:
Australia is drawing a line around AI-generated music.

The Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA) has introduced new eligibility rules barring wholly or largely AI-generated recordings from appearing on the country's official music charts.

Under the updated rules, recordings must be "substantially human made" to qualify for the ARIA Charts. Music created with generative AI in a supporting capacity can still chart, provided that the primary creative work remains human-led and there are no concerns surrounding stream or chart manipulation.

"Wholly AI-generated tracks will not be eligible for the ARIA Charts," ARIA said, adding that recordings using AI "to generate the entirety or the primary portion of the creative elements" will be excluded.

The changes apply to the charts debuting on 28 August.

ARIA CEO Annabelle Herd said the move was intended to protect human creativity while recognising that AI tools are already becoming part of artists' workflows.

"Artists already use AI tools in their work, the Charts can and should evolve to keep room for that, but music generated wholesale by services built on artists' recordings is a different matter," Herd said.

"The ARIA Charts will always remain a transparent measurement of the music Australia consumes, but a chart that rewards unlicensed AI output would undercut the very basis of the recorded music we exist to represent."

Under the new framework, AI can still play a supporting role in a recording. But humans must remain responsible for songwriting, lead vocals, and primary instrumentation, while uses including mastering, drum machines, and Auto-Tune can remain permissible.

Artists will also be required to declare their use of AI when submitting music for chart consideration. If a release is later found to have been largely AI-generated, ARIA can retrospectively adjust its chart position and may request the return of awards issued for a Number One record. Artists and their representatives will also have a process to appeal exclusions.

The rules arrive amid growing debate over AI music

ARIA's decision comes as the music industry continues to grapple with the rapid growth of generative AI.

The issue recently drew attention in Australia following an AI-assisted cover of Madonna's 'Like a Prayer' by Australian DJ Josh Fawaz. The track reached No. 2 on Australia's overall chart and topped the ARIA dance singles chart, while accumulating more than 48 million Spotify streams, according to the BBC.

Fawaz later added generative AI credits to the release following criticism surrounding its use of AI-generated vocals and drums.

Meanwhile, Stereogum reported that streaming service Deezer estimated earlier this year that 44% of tracks being uploaded to its platform were AI-generated.

In the US, AI-generated music remains eligible for the Billboard charts for now. Billboard has instead announced new tools for identifying and labelling AI-generated content, with music data company Luminate set to introduce labels for AI-generated tracks.

Spotify has similarly announced plans for an "AI Persona" badge identifying content producers that are AI-generated rather than real people.

A wider push for "substantially human made" music

Australia's new rules follow principles introduced by the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI), which represents the recording industry internationally.

The IFPI's guidelines similarly state that recordings should be "substantially human made" to qualify for official music charts, with guidelines also set to be introduced across Latin America, the Middle East, Africa, and Southeast Asia.

Australia is not the first country to confront AI-generated releases on its charts. Earlier this year, a song was removed from Sweden's official music charts after it was determined to have been created using AI.

Australian electronic act Peking Duk has also backed ARIA's decision. The duo previously shared an AI-assisted version of their 2014 track 'High', with member Adam Hyde later saying that AI-generated music was "removing the human experience from life".

For ARIA, the new framework isn't designed to eliminate AI from music-making altogether. Instead, it draws a distinction between artists using AI as another tool in their creative process and recordings in which AI effectively becomes the creator.

As Sydney Conservatorium of Music composer and lecturer Alexis Weaver put it, artists can still make use of the technology while "steering the ship and making the main creative choices".

The rules also arrive amid a wider discussion about how artists' work is used to train generative AI systems. In July, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese pledged "the strongest possible protection" for Australian creatives, arguing that writers and musicians should have control over whether their work is used to train AI — and should be compensated when it is.

With AI-generated tracks becoming increasingly common across streaming platforms, Australia's move could offer an early indication of how official charts elsewhere approach one increasingly complicated question: when does a song stop being human-made?

items.body: Honoring its title, Justyna Jablonska‘s Unforeseen never heads exactly where expected; in fact, it’s not even close. The cellist’s debut solo album drips with the confidence of exploration, incorporating multiple genres while acting as a metaphor for the immigrant experience. Jablonska connects the migration of birds with the migration of people and the migration of oft-improvised notes, focusing on the lives of Ukrainian, Polish and Roma Gypsy migrants. While this seems like a lot to tackle, the artist does so with aplomb. The album begins as one might expect a cellist’s album to begin, with sedate phrasing, multitracked lines and a regal tone. The title track demonstrates Jablonska’s depth of emotion while establishing the baseline from which it will soon wander. Were the record to have continued in this vein, it would have remained exemplary; yet the artist strives for something greater, just as those dreaming for a better life might pack their belongings, imitating the flocks passing overhead in the spring and fall. As “If You Can Hear This” launches with a spoken word sample and jungle rhythms, all bets are off. The artist will not be confined by expectation. Is it safe? Not at all, and therein lies the appeal. The bird, the immigrant, the artist may each be called upon to adapt to new surroundings. “9 Daughers” is the first of three vocal pieces, beginning in birdsong and proceeding to a rendition of a traditional Lithuanian folk song A linden tree has nine branches, each one corresponding to a daughter, who each in turn are married, leaving the mother to “sweep the ashes.” The tone is one of mingled celebration and sadness: the empty nest, the broken tree. Can even the birds sing the sorrow away? The next piece starts with the sound of traffic, implying movement; then peaceful kalimba, cello and electronics, each in turn moving the music further away from its origins. The skies open in “Wayward,” and Jablonska seems forlorn, until a series of upbeat melodies are translated to percussion and string. These are the unforeseen joys of leaving the place where one has begun; by the end, the skies have cleared. But not all changes are easy; “Fabryka” introduces a brief note of dissonance, setting the listener up for Monika Niemczynowicz’s return on “The Pact,” an extremely dark cautionary tale from Roztocze, Poland. The presence of such songs underlines the connection between land, culture and memory ~ tales passed down generation to generation, even when the family has migrated to a new home. One hungers for the live show, incorporating film and copious amounts of spoken word, hinted at in the final minute of “Procession.” The album’s greatest surprise arrives toward the end with “Shchedryk (feat. Sofiia Fylypiv).” Most listeners will recognize “Carol of the Bells” in an instant, and many will recall its Ukrainian origins, but few will remember that the song predates Christianity and is about a swallow wishing a family “prosperity, good fortune and a fruitful year.” Jablonska reinstates the original title and meaning, reclaiming it from distortion. This too is a metaphor for the immigrant experience: the temptation to integrate to the extent that one’s history is sublimated. Jablonska, who lives in Glasgow, closes with her own take on “The Skye Boat Song,” which was itself adapted from a Gaelic tune. By the end, one is wondering about the the tug between one’s national origin and country of residence, and the very definition of home. (Richard Allen)

items.body: A label and collective that kept going, kept releasing, kept refining a shared aesthetic without compromise or concession to trends. aux4444 pt.1 carries all of that history in its drum patterns and melodic builds, and it sounds better for it. This is what underground electronic music looks like when it’s done with genuine conviction over a sustained period of time. Fusing IDM and nostalgia that also carries significant electro elements aux4444 pt.1 by omni causa   mind​color​music is a Berlin-based label that has been operating quietly and consistently since 2009 (and previously as a party series), building a catalog of braindance, IDM, jungle, and breakbeat electronica across limited hand-stamped physical releases and digital editions. The label’s naming scheme immediately stands out—every release carries the “aux” prefix followed by a number, a system that applies across all artists on the roster and functions as a unified catalog language rather than individual release titles. aux44 is the name of the series—44 stands for the precinct number of the Berlin Neukölln borough. It’s a clean, distinctive approach that signals something about how the label thinks about its output, not as a collection of individual artist statements but as a continuous ongoing archive (connected to their location) of a shared aesthetic community. The numbers aren’t just catalog codes; they’re evidence of continuity, of a project that has been running long enough to reach four-digit entries. Once you notice it, it catches the eye immediately. ​omni causa—the Berlin-based producer at the center of the mindcolormusic collective, has been releasing material on the label since its earliest releases, with collaborations alongside tysk raider (as Omnibusraider), microlith, fah, and foreign sequence building a catalog that sits consistently in braindance and IDM territory without ever leaning i​nto the acid-heavy, distortion-forward side of the genre. This is melodic and beat-driven braind​ance, loops, breaks, and emotional structure rather than squelching 303 work. aux4444 pt.1 collects material recorded between January 2021 and September 2024, a three-year span tha​t gives the release a sense of accumulated thought rather than a single session document. “Its Relative” is the standout, the most ambitious track on the release in terms of rhythm and structure. The drums carry it entirely. Distorted kicks and a percussion loop hitting in detuned rhythm with what sounds like broken ring modulation applied create a genuinely compelling effect. The melodic builds surrounding that rhythmic core are well placed, surfacing and receding without competing for space. “Perspectives,” the track that follows, is a happy braindance-ish piece where the drum rhythms and bassline work together as something genuinely catchy. The pads build in a way that’s consistent across the album but lands particularly well here. It has a structural and melodic familiarity that recalls how Cylob organized composition on Cylobian Sunset (1996), not in sound, nowhere near what Cylob produces aesthetically, but in the way melody is laid out and the builds are sequenced. That compositional logic, that familiar approach to developing a braindance track from its initial statement toward something larger, is recognizable here and executed with real confidence. The drum work throughout is the album’s strongest consistent element. Break samples fused with analog drum sounds and what sounds like custom electronic percussions tampered enough to matter, it’s a good fusion of IDM and nostalgia that also carries significant electro elements throughout. That electro thread connects aux4444 pt.1 to a lineage of melodic, beat-focused IDM that ran through the Toytronic label in the early 2000s, artists like Multiplex‘s adjacent work, Gimmik‘s more accessible moments, and producers like Bochum Welt, whose warmth and melodic intelligence sat somewhere between electro and IDM without fully committing to either. mindcolormusic has been doing this long enough that reaching the 44 mark in its catalog numbering feels less like a milestone and more like evidence of something quietly remarkable: a label and collective that kept going, kept releasing, kept refining a shared aesthetic without compromise or concession to trends. aux4444 pt.1 carries all of that history in its drum patterns and melodic builds, and it sounds better for it. This is what underground electronic music looks like when it’s done with genuine conviction over a sustained period of time. aux4444 pt.1 is available on mindcolormusic. items.body: On Islands Alight, percussion takes on a structural role, the bass gains weight, echo intervenes in the form, and the pulse alters the relationship between the different parts. The British composer points to the history of dub within electronic music as one of the project’s sources. Entrusting rhythm with a greater share of the tension Islands Alight by James Murray   James Murray arrives at this work after a path in which restraint has become an aesthetic choice even before a technical one. For years, his electronic music has pursued a precise relationship between duration, timbre, and memory. He favors slow construction, minimal variation, and change that acquires meaning over time. The new album brings this approach into more rhythmic territory, shifting the center of gravity of his writing. The transition feels significant precisely because of how naturally it occurs. Murray has long worked with minimal electronic and electroacoustic forms, dense with detail and shaped by a strong awareness of sound. On Islands Alight, percussion takes on a structural role, the bass gains weight, echo intervenes in the form, and the pulse alters the relationship between the different parts. The British composer points to the history of dub within electronic music as one of the project’s sources. It is the most appropriate reference through which to understand this aspect of the album: a culture of space, listening, and studio transformation absorbed into a personal body of research. Four years of work have produced a cohesive record. Continuity is one of its greatest strengths. The London-based musician prefers to work with relationships, allowing an element to change function through what surrounds it. A rhythmic figure gains incisiveness through a minimal shift. A harmonic sequence recedes, allowing a previously secondary detail to emerge. The control is rigorous and almost always discreet. This economy is part of his poetics. Murray places value on restraint, listening, attention to detail, and trust in the person receiving the music. Islands Alight translates these principles into a very concrete form. Passages are given the time they need to develop their function. Resolutions are postponed. Gratification often arrives only after an extended period within the same sonic field, once the relationship between the elements has already altered perception. “Echo alters the memory of what has just happened. Low frequencies establish weight and continuity. Percussion introduces pressure. The synthesizers retain the emotional quality that has long characterized his work. Together, these elements produce music that remains unmistakably his.” ~Mirco Salvadori Rhythm changes this dynamic considerably. It introduces a more pronounced physical dimension and makes the music more mobile. Percussion guides the listening experience with an elastic presence. The pulse moves forward, thins out, then returns with a different weight. Bass affects both depth and the perception of time. Delay and reverb organise distance, duration, and density. The effects belong to the composition just as much as the harmonic parts do. The relationship with the history of dub can be measured above all through this method. Murray takes certain production principles and brings them into his own language. The studio becomes part of the writing process. Echo alters the memory of what has just happened. Low frequencies establish weight and continuity. Percussion introduces pressure. The synthesizers retain the emotional quality that has long characterized his work. Together, these elements produce music that remains unmistakably his. Islands Alight retains a strong connection with his recent history. Weeds had already demonstrated how detail could become structure and how limited variation could acquire emotional significance. His work with Ian Hawgood confirmed his ability to treat sonic material with extreme patience. The new record introduces a different kind of mobility. The writing appears more sensitive to weight, entrusting rhythm with a greater share of the tension. The environmental theme identified by the artist also enters into this perspective. Murray has linked the record to heatwaves, drought, and a form of ecological anxiety connected to the present. These references operate as an internal pressure within the project. The titles evoke waters, islands, calms, marine animals, and currents. They provide essential coordinates while keeping meaning open. The music proceeds according to its own logic, allowing those images to operate at a deeper level. Murray builds tension using limited means :: The cover follows the same sense of restraint. The original photograph is transformed until color, material, and folds become its dominant features. With only a few elements, the image suggests change and fragility. Its connection with the record is immediate precisely because of its sobriety. The most interesting quality of this album lies in the way Murray manages continuity. Duration makes minute transformations perceptible. The music demands concentration, yet soon reveals a very clear internal scale. A detail that initially seems marginal can acquire prominence several minutes later. A pulse can change its function through a simple shift in context. In this way, Murray builds tension using limited means. Melody retains a decisive role. The harmonies possess the controlled melancholy already present in his previous work, but here they are exposed differently to rhythm, bass, and effects. The production follows the same principle. Definition is high, the detail carefully handled, and depth meticulously managed. The technical work maintains an evident musical function. Murray uses control to give the individual elements autonomy and to make small differences in weight and intensity perceptible. Even in the densest passages, the sound remains clear and readable. Such rigorous control also entails an element of risk. Some passages display a highly regulated timbral continuity, leaving less room for the unexpected. Yet this choice is entirely consistent with the character of a record that demands time and a willingness to engage with slowness. Its idea of movement develops through persistence and internal variation. Some listeners may find this discipline severe. It is also the point at which James Murray expresses his concept of composition most clearly. Trust in the listener therefore becomes central. The record offers few explicit signals and allows meaning to emerge through duration. Some elements gain importance when they disappear. Others appear almost motionless, yet change their function through a new rhythmic relationship. Complexity presents itself with great discretion. Complexity presents itself with great discretion :: This makes Islands Alight a significant work within Murray’s discography. It brings together melodic sensitivity, an interest in electroacoustic material, precision in sound design, and a rhythmic investigation developed with particular depth. The influence of dub history expands the tools at his disposal and shapes his treatment of space, pulse, and the studio. The ambient dimension continues to inform his sensibility, in keeping with the open and undogmatic definition Murray himself has always preferred for his music. The result possesses a particular strength because it avoids the need to announce its change. Islands Alight works as an internal development. Elements that have long been present find a different proportion and produce new consequences. Murray knows his own language well and modifies its rules with precision. The title itself contributes to this impression: two words containing ideas of light, heat, exposure, and a mental geography reduced to a few signs. The environmental anxiety identified by the artist adds another layer of tension. Murray allows it to operate beneath the surface of the work. The beauty of the record often arises from this caution, from its ability to suggest a problem through form rather than turning it into a declaration. Islands Alight works as an internal development. Elements that have long been present find a different proportion and produce new consequences. Murray knows his own language well and modifies its rules with precision. ~Mirco Salvadori After repeated listening, the maturity of the project becomes clear: this is the work of a musician deepening his own vocabulary and changing the way it behaves. The rhythmic component opens new possibilities, the attention to detail preserves its coherence, and the emotional dimension finds a more physical balance. Islands Alight seems to define a precise phase in his artistic trajectory. Murray’s poetry emerges from his control of material and his trust in time. A small number of decisions can transform an entire passage. A sound acquires meaning through position, duration, and memory. This precision gives the record an intense yet measured presence. Islands Alight is one of the most accomplished works of James Murray’s recent career. A focused, patient album, capable of expanding his research through rhythm, space, and studio transformation. Murray’s voice remains perfectly recognisable and here finds a new substance. Islands Alight is available on quiet details. items.body: Simon Heath closes the release notes with “May you rest in peace.” There’s nothing to add to that. The Yasu Ether Project is an overall haunting and pleasant experience, a final document of an artist who understood that darkness and stillness aren’t opposites of beauty but conditions under which a particular kind of beauty becomes possible. César Alexandre knew that instinctively, and this album proves it one last time. A quiet closing chapter The Yasu Ether Project by Mount Shrine   Cryo Chamber has held the bar for exploratory dark ambient music with a cinematic edge since Simon Heath (the artist behind Atrium Carceri) founded the label with a collaborative focus that has become its defining characteristic. The catalog spans deep space drone, horror-influenced soundscapes, Lovecraftian collaborative projects, and the kind of patient, immersive dark ambient that rewards extended, solitary listening. Among its most beloved artists was Mount Shrine—the project of César Alexandre, a Brazilian producer from Rio de Janeiro who grew up absorbing Brian Eno, Burial, Aphex Twin, and Akira Yamaoka‘s score for Silent Hill 2 before finding his own voice in lo-fi field recordings, vinyl crackle, tape hiss, and long meditative drone structures. He debuted on Cryo Chamber with Winter Restlessness in 2018, followed by Ghosts on Broken Pavements in 2019. He also worked under Mount Hibiki and released vaporwave under the name Lindsheaven Virtual Plaza, an early and influential figure in that scene. César Alexandre passed away on April 15, 2021, from COVID-19. He was one of the first artists whose work made people fall in love with ambient music, and the void he left has been felt consistently in the years since. Cryo Chamber has honored his memory carefully—releasing All Roads Lead Home in 2022 and The Mount Hibiki Tapes in 2024, and The Yasu Ether Project arrives now as the final piece of audio he ever sent to Simon Heath. A version had previously appeared on his own Bandcamp before the page closed. Now preserved and released once more, it stands as a quiet closing chapter. There is a somber feeling that comes with reading about this release before you press play, and that feeling doesn’t leave once you do. Listening to this is the last remnant of his feelings and emotions, the final transmission from an artist whose music offered rest, solitude, and quiet escape to everyone who found it. Just like most Cryo Chamber releases you can expect a very dark and soft ride through the entirety of the album, but there is something that peaks through all the darkness, a simple peace that is haunting. You don’t know what it is that’s calming about it. Maybe it’s the field recordings of birds and daytime, the remembrance of what it feels like when you’ve just woken from a bad storm. Unsettling and peaceful at the same time. That’s how it feels listening to this. Unsettling and peaceful at the same time :: “Gaseous Peak” and “Polysunset” are the standouts on this release. The entirety of the album is wrapped in vinyl hiss, that persistent crackle that was always central to Mount Shrine‘s identity, the sound of something being played back from a medium that’s been worn down by time. It gives the record a physical texture, a sense that these recordings exist in a material world even as the music itself drifts away from one. The closing track is something different. The synths here aren’t just simple pads and atmospheric textures like the rest of the album. Little vocal touches, small nothings, barely registered, appear as the pads build. A small key arp plays in and out, and the visual being created in your head as you listen is genuinely peaceful in a way that feels earned after everything that preceded it. The contradiction at the heart of this closing track is what makes it so affecting, the familiar Mount Shrine darkness is still present, but something lighter has been let in, a crack of warmth that sits differently knowing what this release represents. Simon Heath closes the release notes with “May you rest in peace.” There’s nothing to add to that. The Yasu Ether Project is an overall haunting and pleasant experience, a final document of an artist who understood that darkness and stillness aren’t opposites of beauty but conditions under which a particular kind of beauty becomes possible. César Alexandre knew that instinctively, and this album proves it one last time. The Yasu Ether Project is available on Cryo Chamber. items.body: Arca’s latest record pushes her glitch-heavy, genre-defying sound further than ever, turning chaos, vulnerability, and radical experimentation into one of her most fearless works yet. Arca turns chaos into art Throughout her career, Arca has been moving in and out of pop and radical experimentation. If you’ve seen her in concert, you probably know how chaotic it can get, often slipping into the multimedia with a feral mix of live music, DJ-ing, and performance art. A heart-rending a cappella rendition of “Piel” from her 2017 self titled will follow a reggaeton classic, then Aphex Twin’s infamous “Ventolin” will play while she squirts paint on plexiglass and behind her, her face distorts in a thousand ways in glitched up videos. Just in the past year, she’s gone from working on music with mainstay names—producing for none other than Madonna in her return to form Confessions II and remixing for Robyn and Nine Inch Nails—to her first art exhibitions including at the ICA in London, to a new instalment of her NTS project Airdoll. A new album and/or mixtape had been teased for some time now, following a break after the five-part Kick project. Airdoll—aired just two weeks before the release of XXXXX, and a few days before its announcement—showed a glimpse of things to come: a radio mix of largely own music, it included tracks from her previou​s uncategorisable releases @@@@@, ±±±±±, and Disintegrator alongside unreleased music. The flow and selection in Airdoll hinted at a complex, chaotic and experimental direction, in direct contrast to the laser-focused styles of Kick II to V and the accessibility of Puta/Sola. Last year’s double-single, in fact, was widely assumed to be the start of a new album cycle, however XXXXX does not include any previously released material, nor was it preceded by any singles. Rather, it dropped like a bolt out of the ether, or, as album opener “No End” states kicking off the diva experimental FM transmission, it “cut through the horizon with piercing hope”. Swelling strings follow, and pulsing industrial beats, and voices so processed to feel barely human in tracks flowing one into the other with no solution of continuity. It’s clear from the beginning that this album returns to the freeform exploration of earlier Arca releases such as &&&&& and Xen—the intense emotional quality of “Wound” is right there at the onset in “Willow,” with its strings soaring atop a likely sample of the bells from Aphex’s “XMD 5a”—but the truth is that it’s hard to compare XXXXX to anything other than Arca herself, bringing her craft to a logical peak. While some connections to her previous work and to others can be made, such as the aforementioned Aphex, or SOPHIE’s or Autechre’s outrageous sound design (the “Heart”/“Syncope”/“Raver” trifecta a wonderful case in point), or even the nod to Daddy Yankee’s “Rompe” in “Eidolon,” the album is a probing journey into the unknown, led by faith in the human. “Cinch,” the first of a few minute-long narrative respites in XXXXX’s torrential flow, makes this abundantly clear: “And so she wandered beyond the threshold, moving further still into the unknown. Eyes closed. Heart open.” The traveler, merged with a technology of her own making in the Gigerian album cover, has no fear. One of the album’s highlights, the maximalist “Fxck” pushes pop’s catchiness into the extremes of deconstructed club, with a changa tuki propulsor and post-industrial sound design, crude hi-hats bouncing left and right in the stereo field while sub synth surges anchor lyrics on rough sex as a way to kill the Freudian father. “Taconeando” takes the opposite approach, with a bare and dry take on KicK iii’s warped hip hop influence. These two moments at the heart of the album, probably the closest to songs the album has to offer, pave the way to a latter section drifting into emotional and electrifying IDM, with “Grip” offering one of the record’s most passionate and memorable melodies—a piano progression (Arca’s acoustic instrument of choice) on top of dryly cut and harshly flanging synths—and “Everything” almost slipping into flash-core aesthetics with its relentlessness. The album closes on a harrowing and ambiguous note with “Sueño,” a strident number where a raptor voice so distorted it becomes a synth begs to stop, turn away, turn it off. The voice/synth glitches once more into self-reference, duetting with and bleeding into a sample of Arca’s own unreleased demo “Arpia,” or harpy. A frequent proponent of the glitch as philosophy of art and of life, Arca has slit through innumerable systems such as artistic discipline, genre, gender and taste. XXXXX itself glitched from the mixtape format to album status, just like @@@@@ had glitched into the single format, and its tracks happily blip in and out of themselves and their meanings and feelings. The technology bringing on the glitch is that of the Diva: an archetype—half mythological, half psychoanalytical—holding it all together by a golden thread. A Pallas redux, goddess of art, craft and knowledge, warlike and just and now enhanced into the biomechanoid future, riding an impossible spacecraft, escorted by owls. It’s easy to fail to convey her, to not come through with words as a substitute to sound. As Minerva’s owls only spread their wings with the falling of dusk, the glitch is unpredicted, and only fully understandable after the fact. XXXXX is available on XL. [Bandcamp]  The post Arca :: XXXXX (XL) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Six tracks, no wasted motion. ARKADA005 doesn’t revive electro; it plugs it back in, turns the voltage up, and lets the machine speak for itself. Drawing on the foundational grammar of electro Marking a welcome return to the furor of contemporary electronic music, London’s Arkada resurfaces with ARKADA005, a six-track workout from Brussels’ Arsonist Recorder and Sigma_ALgebra. This is electro with the futurist chrome stripped back enough to expose the working parts: rolling bass, snapping breaks, brutal low-end pressure and melodies that still know how to carry a tune. The record feels contemporary without straining to prove it, drawing on the foundational grammar of electro while treating that grammar as ​something alive, flexible and available for further damage. Arsonist Recorder takes the first three cuts straight to the machine soul. The rhythms are tight but never sterile, with heavyweight bass movement and synth lines that bring a real sense of propulsion. There is funk here, but it is not nostalgia-funk. It is the physical intelligence of the form: music built to make the body respond while the circuitry does something stranger underneath. Sigma_ALgebra with three tracks that feel like an autopsy performed at club volume. The components are stripped down, isolated and rebuilt into lean, muscular constructions where breaks, bass and synthetic detail lock together with increasingly brutal efficiency. What makes the record work is the tension between its opposing instincts—sweet melody and hard mechanics, precision and abrasion, body-popping unity and 4am chicanery. Six tracks, no wasted motion. ARKADA005 doesn’t revive electro; it plugs it back in, turns the voltage up, and lets the machine speak for itself. Arkada #005 is available on Arkada.
